Town Of Plattsburgh To Receive Fed Support After Schumer Brought US Army Corps Of Engineers To Meet With Town About How To Deal With Critical Infrastructure Left From The Former Air Force Base Following Schumer’s Advocacy, Town of Plattsburgh Added To Lake Champlain Basin Program Unlocking Critical Opportunities For Inventorying And Remediation Funding; Senator Vows To Fight To Reauthorize Critical Program In Upcoming Bill Schumer: Investing In Lake Champlain Conservation Program Is A WIN – WIN That Will Help Protect Both The Lake And Town Residents Following his advocacy , U.S. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer today announced that the Town of Plattsburgh has been added to the Lake Champlain Basin Program (LCBP), which unlocked new federal funding opportunities that will help the Town fix crumbling infrastructure at the former Air Force Base. Schumer previously secured a meeting between Town of Plattsburgh officials and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers to assess the condition and scope of the base’s Cold War-era infrastructure. Schumer said that meeting directly led to the Town’s inclusion in the LCBP that will help the Town secure necessary federal investment to inventory and begin to address the outdated infrastructure. Schumer also launched his push to reauthorize the critical federal program that supports Lake Champlain and its surrounding area. “For decades, Plattsburgh Air Force Base played a vital role in protecting our country during the Cold War. Now, with Plattsburgh International Airport, it continues its service to the North Country as a travel hub for Northern New Yorkers. However, its Cold War-era infrastructure is falling apart, creating sinkholes and sending unwanted sediments into Lake Champlain, and locals are concerned the next storm could bring more damage,” said Senator Schumer. “That’s why I was proud to ensure the Town of Plattsburgh was added to the Lake Champlain Basin Program so we can unlock new federal funding to assess and inventory the infrastructure and provide a funding source for future remediation of the crumbling drainage system. As Congress begins to work on our next water funding bill, I am thinking of the Town of Plattsburgh as I fight to reauthorize this vital program for the Lake Champlain region.” Plattsburgh Air Force Base closed three decades ago, and much of the infrastructure was installed when the base was built in the mid-1950s. When the base closed, the town had concerns that the infrastructure built by the Air Force may not be up to current standards. Since then, pipes that were designed to drain water away from the flight line are collapsing due to heavy rains, creating sinkholes, sending unwanted and likely contaminated sediments into Lake Champlain, and creating concern that more damage could be coming. “A town of our size could easily be overwhelmed by a project of this magnitude. We would never have the financial resources to begin studying the problem, let alone start the actual construction process to rehabilitate the failing infrastructure left behind when the Airbase closed. We are deeply appreciative of the connections that Senator Schumer has made on our behalf. His involvement in the process has been invaluable and is a testament to his commitment to the North Country. The importance of this project to the continued economic development of the former Plattsburgh Air Force Base cannot be overstated. This is a project with a generational impact that will ensure a sustainable future for an extremely vital portion of the Town of Plattsburgh,” said Supervisor Chuck Kostyk, Town of Plattsburgh. Last year, U.S. Senator Chuck Schumer secured a meeting in Plattsburgh between Town officials and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers regarding the former Air Force Base. Michael Cashman, then serving as Town Supervisor, had asked Schumer for assistance in assessing the condition and scope of the Cold War-era infrastructure, and the senator worked for weeks to help get the USACE to agree to send out a team of engineers to see the site, now operating commercial flights as Plattsburgh International Airport, firsthand and provide technical expertise as the town evaluates next steps. The Army Corps, with Schumer’s support, then helped ensure the Town of Plattsburgh’s inclusion in the LCBP to unlock federal funding opportunities to conduct a $650,000 study to assess and inventory the infrastructure and potentially remediate the problem. The LCBP and its Lake Champlain Watershed Environmental Assistance Program support New York and Vermont’s efforts to improve Lake Champlain’s water quality, support wildlife habitat, and enhance the environment throughout the lake’s watershed. Schumer has a long history of supporting the LCBP. Schumer has cosponsored numerous bills to support the foundation, growth, and continued funding of the LCBP. Apart from fighting to secure the program funding through annual appropriations bills, Schumer also secured an additional $40 million in funding as part of his Bipartisan Infrastructure & Jobs Law. Back in 2024, under Schumer’s leadership in the Senate, economically disadvantaged communities like Plattsburgh only have to provide a 10% local cost share, down from the previous level of 35%. This year, he proudly cosponsored the LCBP Enhancements Act of 2026 , which would reauthorize the program and maintain its funding through 2032, improve oversight of the program’s fiscal agent to ensure funds are administered in a timely and proper manner, and formally authorize the partnership between the LCBP and the Great Lakes Fishery Commission (GLFC), allowing for greater support for Lake Champlain. Additionally, Schumer is pushing to increase funding for LCBP through the Fiscal Year 2027 Interior Appropriations bill. This funding is critical to restore, protect, and prevent pollution of the Lake Champlain ecosystem and also to plan responses for climate-related disasters. Schumer today launched his push to reauthorize the LCBP in the upcoming bipartisan Water Resources Development Act (WRDA), so the program can continue its mission while working with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) to make its grants more accessible to the local communities and dedicated partners on the shore like the Town of Plattsburgh. Schumer has delivered many millions of dollars in federal funding to support Plattsburgh, Clinton County, and the Plattsburgh Airport. Through the American Rescue Plan, Schumer delivered millions of dollars in federal funding to help Clinton County recover from the COVID-19 pandemic, including $15.61 million for Clinton County, $2.14 million for the City of Plattsburgh, and $1.31 million for the Town of Plattsburgh. Schumer has delivered millions of dollars for Plattsburgh International Airport, including $184,000 from the Airport Improvement Program just last year, $1.4 million from the Airport Improvement Program in 2024, and nearly $6 million for various projects through the Airport Improvement Grant program. Schumer earlier this year also successfully increased funding for the vital Essential Air Service program Plattsburgh International Airport relies on, providing $514 million for the EAS program – a nearly 15% increase from last year, rejecting President Trump’s proposal to cut the program by 50% and preventing the Department of Transportation from haphazardly terminating any EAS contracts. ###

Fort Drum Will Be Home To Next-Generation Nuclear Microreactor To Protect Domestic Military Bases From Grid Failures, Critical Energy Deficiencies, And Other Threats Earlier This Month, Schumer Urged The Army To Pick Fort Drum To Demonstrate Safe And Secure, On-Site Nuclear Power Generation Schumer: Fort Drum Will Lead The Next Frontier In Nuclear Power! After calling on U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll to pick Fort Drum for a next-generation nuclear power program , U.S. Senator Chuck Schumer today announced the Army heeded his call and has selected Fort Drum to spearhead the Janus Program and the Army’s nuclear energy innovation. Schumer explained that the Army will deploy a commercial nuclear microreactor to strengthen the installation’s energy resilience and ability to support military operations on post. Ensuring military sites have secure, reliable power if the commercial power grid goes down is critical for the Army’s readiness. Fort Drum is uniquely qualified to help the Army meet its nuclear energy goals due to its infrastructure, power projection capability, and the 10 th Mountain Division’s mission requirements. “As a steadfast supporter and fierce advocate of Fort Drum, I’m proud to announce that the Army heeded my call, selecting Fort Drum to spearhead the deployment of nuclear microreactor technology in the North Country. This is a major win that will strengthen the base’s energy security, protect our Army from grid failures, and reduce strain on the local power grid,” said Senator Schumer. “As one of our nation’s most advanced and strategic military installations, the critical missions Fort Drum supports and executes to advance our national defense require safe and secure, as well as reliable and resilient, onsite power generation. That is why Fort Drum is perfectly poised to lead the next frontier in nuclear power, and I commend the Army for recognizing this and selecting Fort Drum.” The Department of the Army’s Janus Program is an initiative to deploy commercially-owned and operated nuclear microreactors on certain domestic Army installations by 2030. Through the deployment of these microreactors, the program will help strengthen the Army’s installation energy resilience, support evolving mission requirements, and advance the military’s adoption of nuclear energy. Last year, the Army announced that nine military installations—including Fort Drum—were shortlisted for consideration to host a commercial nuclear microreactor under the Janus Program. This week, the Army announced that Fort Drum and four other installations were selected and paired with vendors for the first round of microreactor deployments under the Janus Program. Schumer earlier this month, in a letter to U.S. Secretary of the Army Dan Driscoll, explained that Fort Drum—home to Wheeler-Sack Army Airfield and the 10 th Mountain Division, the most deployed conventional Army unit since 2001—is one of the most strategic military installations and power projection capabilities in the United States. A nuclear microreactor would provide Fort Drum with a reliable, independent, and continuous source of energy for mission-critical support functions, command and control elements, mobilization activities, and other vital capabilities, including during grid-level energy infrastructure outages. Schumer added that Fort Drum’s location would allow the Army to assess a microreactor’s performance under harsh weather and other conditions needed to inform its efforts to integrate energy solutions into future operations. Schumer also explained Fort Drum currently uses approximately 60 megawatts of power, most of which is pulled from the local grid. Fort Drum is a vital economic and community anchor for the North Country, supporting thousands of military and civilian jobs. Fort Drum is well-equipped to demonstrate how nuclear power can reduce vulnerabilities and reinforce critical U.S. defense infrastructure. It is expected that the commercial microreactor would not require significant land use changes and would be designed to produce up to 20 megawatts (MW) of power to support installation operations. Fort Drum officials and the local community have conveyed support for the site’s selection for the Janus Program. Across decades of service as Fort Drum’s leading champion in Congress, Schumer has fought tirelessly to elevate Fort Drum and the 10 th Mountain Division to US Department of Defense and Army leadership, and the Senator has proudly delivered billions of dollars in federal funding to enhance Fort Drum’s capabilities and readiness, upgrade outdated infrastructure, add thousands of new personnel, and safeguard the future of the North Country’s pillar of national defense and primary economic engine for generations to come. Last year, after personally meeting with 10 th Mountain Division Commanding General Scott Naumann and Army Secretary Dan Driscoll to push for critical upgrades to Wheeler-Sack Army Airfield, Schumer landed $18 million in federal funding as a downpayment on the long-overdue modernization of the airfield’s lighting and electrical system , which currently uses components that date as far back as the 1950s and are far beyond the end of their useful life. The year prior, Schumer fought for and delivered $18.5 million in the Senate’s Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA) for the planning and design of a new aircraft maintenance hangar and an Operational Readiness Training Complex at Fort Drum. Schumer also secured nearly $10 million in the FY2023 end-of-year spending package for the planning and design of a new physical fitness testing facility field house, and to modernize one of the installation’s key Access Control Points (ACP). In 2022, after a series of personal appeals to former Army Secretary Christine Wormuth and announcing that Fort Drum was selected as a finalist , Schumer successfully secured one of the Army’s prestigious Multi-Domain Task Force (MDTF) for Fort Drum. That same year, after personal calls to former Army Secretary Mark Esper and Army Chief of Staff James McConville , the Senator successfully secured over $27 million in federal funding to construct a new railhead at Fort Drum and replace the installation’s existing water supply , which was vulnerable to multiple forms of contamination. Schumer was also proud to fight for and deliver more than $21 million for a new Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) Hangar in 2020, $19 million in funding for a new non-commissioned officer (NCO) training academy in 2015, and many more exciting wins in support of Fort Drum, the 10 th Mountain Division, and the brave men and women who serve there. ###

“Bonus Buy” Will Help Local Western NY Farmers After Major NY Grape Processor Abruptly Canceled Contracts Earlier This Year After They Had Already Invested In Preparing Their Vineyards For The Season Last Week Schumer Stood With Western New York Grape Farmers And Called On USDA To Use Authority To Purchase Excess Grapes For Domestic Food Assistance Programs & Help Keep Upstate Concord Grape Farmers Growing Schumer, Gillibrand: Grape Purchase Is Win-Win For Local Farmers And Putting American-Grown Grapes To Good Use After Schumer stood with Western New York grape farmers just last week – after their contracts for this season were suddenly terminated – to call on the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to purchase Concord grape juice for use by domestic nutrition programs across the country, U.S. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand today announced the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) has heeded their call and will purchase $20 million in surplus product to ensure the continued success of Concord grape growers in New York. Earlier this year, Refresco suddenly canceled contracts with approximately 126 farmers across New York and Pennsylvania after they had already invested in preparing their vineyards for this season, leaving local growers in a lurch. The senators explained today’s announcement provides much-needed relief for Western New York grape farmers who were facing growing uncertainty amid rising costs and the loss of a major client. “Everyone knows the best Concord grapes come from Upstate New York. But when Refresco cancelled contracts with many grape farmers earlier this year, growers were left in a lurch with nowhere to sell their harvests. That’s why, last week, I stood shoulder to shoulder with Western New York grape farmers in Chautauqua County and urged the USDA to buy extra Concord grape juice for nutrition programs,” said Senator Schumer. “I’m proud to announce that USDA has heeded my call to purchase Concord grape juice. This is a win for Upstate farmers, families, and New York’s economy. I’ll keep fighting for our growers and a stronger domestic food supply chain.” “Earlier this year, New York State Concord grape farmers were left stranded after having their contracts suddenly canceled,” said Senator Gillibrand. “That is why I called on the USDA to step in and purchase surplus Concord grape juice for federal nutrition programs. I am thrilled that the USDA answered our call by enacting Section 32 of the Agricultural Adjustment Act to support Western New York’s growers during this critical time. This decision delivers relief to our local farming families and protects a critical part of New York’s agricultural economy." Chautauqua County is the leading grape-producing county in the state and the largest grape-growing county in the country outside of California. Every year, about 800 growers produce 150,000 tons or more of grapes on more than 22,000 acres on the Lake Erie Plain across northern Pennsylvania and Western New York. Products like juices and jellies that come from Concord grapes are processed locally and sold across the world. The Cornell Cooperative Extension estimates that the Lake Erie Grape Belt region supports about 2,000 jobs, contributes upwards of $300 million in economic impact, and supports a fruit and vegetable processing industry that employs over 5,000 workers. Western New York’s grape sector is an economic anchor for the state’s agricultural industry, as Lake Erie’s shallow depth extends the growing season by moderating temperatures as it keeps air moving when grapes are at risk for frost. The region extends far beyond Chautauqua County. Niagara County is home to the Niagara Escarpment American Viticultural Area, which contains nearly 60 farms across more than 1,000 acres of vineyard. The Niagara grape was created in Niagara County by cross-breeding Concord and Cassady grapes and is now a staple for making white grape juice. In March, Refresco, a major processor for many New York grape farmers, canceled all of its contracts with grape growers. Refresco bought from 126 grape growers across New York and Pennsylvania in the Lake Erie region. Since then, New York’s grape growers have been struggling in the face of an uncertain future. In early June, over two months ago, Schumer sent a letter to USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins and explained that purchasing grapes for use by domestic nutrition programs would alleviate stress for Concord grape growers in Western New York. Section 32 funds, which are the source of funding for the grape buy announced today, are authorized by Section 32 of the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 and used by USDA to purchase agricultural products, which are in turn used for nutrition programs such as the school lunch program. These “bonus buys” have been used by USDA in the past to stabilize agricultural markets, support communities, and deliver nutritious food to those who need it most. In fact, earlier this year, Schumer and Gillibrand fought to secure exactly such a purchase by USDA to stabilize prices for New York grape farmers. Section 32 has also been deployed successfully for Concord grapes in 2006, 2007, 2009, 2014, 2017, and 2024. ###

West Kill Post Office Has Served the Local Community Since 1833 , But Was Temporarily Closed In January 2025 After Fire Shut Down Small Rural Office – And Postal Services Have Not Yet Returned, Forcing Customers To Travel Over Seven Miles Away To Shandaken To Collect Mail Schumer Urges USPS To Fully Restore Postal Operations So Residents Can Easily Receive Medications, Checks & Bills, Packages, And Other Important Mail Schumer To USPS: West Kill Deserves A Post Office In West Kill A year and a half after a fire forced the closure of the West Kill Post Office, with no communicated plan for reinstatement , U.S. Senator Chuck Schumer called on the United States Postal Service (USPS) to work with the local community and fully restore mail services to the hamlet. The West Kill Post Office has served the Greene County hamlet for nearly two centuries, and Schumer said it provides a vital service to residents and the community. For years, Schumer has fought relentlessly to protect post offices across Upstate New York, demanding accountability from the U.S. Postal Service, ensuring rural residents have a voice in decisions that affect them, and defending the local institutions that keep small communities connected. “The West Kill Post Office is more than a place to pick up and drop off mail. For nearly two centuries, it’s been a community hub for residents. Upstate New Yorkers rely on their local post office to receive medications, pay bills, and connect with the rest of the world. But since a fire shut down the post office more than a year and a half ago, to receive mail, residents have been forced to travel over seven miles along a remote highway that lacks cell service and is dangerous to travel in the winter months,” said Senator Schumer . “Every day this post office remains closed, the community of West Kill is deprived of an essential service. For a year and a half, the West Kill community has been asking for answers but has heard nothing. West Kill deserves transparency and action, which is why I’m calling on the USPS to work with residents to immediately reinstate postal service in the town.” In January 2025, a fire forced the USPS to close the West Kill Post Office. For the past year and a half, hundreds of residents have been forced to travel 7.3 miles to access in-person mail services at an alternate site at the Shandaken Post Office. This is a dangerous drive along the remote stretch of State Route 42 through the Deep Notch, which has no cell service and is hard to travel in the winter. Residents have been willing to work constructively with USPS and local officials to find a solution but still lack a clear timeline or meaningful explanation regarding when and where full postal services will return to West Kill. They have emphasized the importance of the post office as a crucial community space , providing important services like access to prescription drugs, hunting and fishing licensing, electric vehicle charging, and Wi-Fi access. Schumer said the USPS must fully and transparently work with the community to restore full mail services in the town. Schumer’s letter to USPS Postmaster General David Steiner can be found HERE or below: Dear Postmaster General Steiner, I write with concern regarding the future of the West Kill Post Office, located at 30 Spruceton Rd, West Kill, NY 12492. It has come to my attention that in January 2025, the United States Postal Service (USPS) issued a temporary closure of the West Kill Post Office, citing smoke damage at the location. Since then, residents of West Kill have been forced to travel over seven miles to access in-person retail mail services. I urge you to act swiftly and diligently to immediately reinstate the West Kill Post Office and restore full mail services in West Kill, whether through a timely restoration of the existing location at West Kill or through securing an alternative location nearby in West Kill. Furthermore, I urge you to act with full transparency and cooperation in engaging the West Kill community on the Postal Service’s plans for reinstating the West Kill Post Office. The West Kill community deserves answers as to the future of their post office – and the USPS must act in full faith and transparency to provide the community with the answers it deserves, and work in close conjunction with the community in determining the future of the West Kill Post Office. For over a year and a half, the hundreds of residents in West Kill, a hamlet in the Town of Lexington, have been forced to travel 7.3 miles to access in-person mail services at an alternate site at the Shandaken Post Office, located at 22 State Route 42, Shandaken, NY 12480. This is a dangerous drive along the remote stretch of State Route 42 through the Deep Notch, which has no cell service and is hard to travel in the winter. The residents of West Kill have been harmed by the Postal Service’s delay in reopening the West Kill Post Office for far too long. Any further delay in reinstating the West Kill Post Office is unacceptable – the Postal Service must immediately act to reopen the West Kill Post Office such that the residents of West Kill will no longer have to face severe challenges to pick up their medications, receive their checks and billing documents, and other important mail. The West Kill community has also demonstrated its willingness to work constructively with USPS and local officials to find a solution. After more than a year and a half, however, residents still lack a clear timeline or meaningful explanation regarding when and where full postal services will return to West Kill. USPS must provide the community with a concrete plan and commitment to restoring local postal services. Therefore, I urge you to immediately act to reinstate the West Kill Post Office in West Kill, NY, and fully and transparently communicate and engage with the West Kill community on the future of the West Kill Post Office. Thank you for your attention to this important matter. I look forward to hearing your response. ###

Schumer Says Tariff Costs, Shifting Consumer Trends, And Distribution Disruptions Threaten Upstate New York’s Craft Beverage Industry Senator Backs New York Wine & Grape Foundation’s $500,000 SBA Proposal To Strengthen Supply Chain Resilience Schumer: Support Upstate New York’s Craft Beverage Industry U.S. Senator Chuck Schumer earlier this week convened leaders from craft breweries, wineries, distilleries, and other industries at the Schuyler County Business Park to discuss the growing challenges facing the industry, including changing consumption trends, rising costs from tariffs, and distribution disruptions that are all straining the supply chain. Schumer emphasized that these pressures are hitting small- and mid-sized producers particularly hard and could have a significant impact on rural communities across Upstate New York that rely on craft beverage businesses to support farms, tourism, and restaurants. “New York’s craft breweries, wineries, and distilleries are a cornerstone of Upstate’s economy, and I have fought for years to help these small businesses grow and reach new markets. Today, costs from unwise tariffs, changing consumer trends, and major logistical disruptions are making doing business even harder and putting that progress at risk. That’s why I’m backing the New York Wine & Grape Foundation’s collaborative effort to strengthen our regional supply chain and help producers weather and overcome these challenges,” said Senator Schumer. “New York’s craft beverage industry has been brewing success for years, especially in the Finger Lakes, and we’re not going to let these challenges knock it flat. I’ll keep fighting to make sure Upstate New York’s craft beverage businesses have the federal support they need to navigate these challenges and continue to strengthen local economies.” New York’s craft beverage industry has consistently grown in recent years. According to the New York State Brewers Association (NYSBA), the number of breweries in New York grew from 95 in 2012 to more than 500 in 2024. New York is now the nation’s second-largest craft beer market, with an estimated $4.8 billion economic impact, while annual craft brewery production increased from 557,436 barrels in 2011 to 1,434,992 barrels in 2023. New York is also the third-largest wine-producing state in the nation, behind only California and Washington. New York’s wine and grape industries are a major economic engine as well. According to the New York Wine & Grape Foundation’s latest annual report , the state’s wine and grape industries have directly generated more than $16.81 billion in direct economic impact. Nigar Hale, Executive Director of The Watkins Glenn Area Chamber of Commerce, said, “ Craft beverage is woven into the fabric of our rural economy, supporting local farms, tourism, restaurants, and small businesses. We’re facing real challenges, particularly within the distribution side of the supply chain. I appreciate that the Senator took the time to seek out our perspective and listen to the challenges we’re facing firsthand. It was a valuable opportunity to continue the dialogue and work toward solutions.” Ian Conboy, Lucky Hare Brewing Company, said , “New York’s craft breweries are manufacturers, employers, tourism destinations, and important parts of our communities. Rising costs for aluminum, ingredients, and equipment continue to put pressure on small independent breweries. We appreciate Senator Schumer listening to New York brewers and working to ensure federal policy supports American manufacturers and keeps our industry strong.” Rick Rainey, Forge Cellars, said, “ The New York wine industry has a substantial economic impact for the state of New York and all of the residents. Senator Schumer’s efforts to help bring more New York wine to more New Yorkers is a big win-win for our state and can have far reaching positive impact. #NYdrinksNY” Schumer said the industry is facing continued uncertainty from counterproductive U.S. tariffs that raise the cost of cans, packaging, equipment, and other inputs for New York craft producers. The latest threat of additional 50% tariffs on Canadian imports has created additional uncertainty, raising costs and making it harder for businesses to plan ahead. Schumer has long worked with local vineyards and the New York Wine & Grape Foundation to increase export access to Canada, including Ontario’s Liquor Control Board of Ontario (LCBO), one of the largest single wine buyers in the world. Historically, his work helped Finger Lakes wines reach LCBO shelves in recent years, unlocking an important market for New York producers. In part, thanks to Schumer’s efforts, Canada had become the largest market for American wine outside the U.S., making continued access to Canadian consumers especially important for New York’s wine industry. However, in response to the Trump administration’s reckless tariffs in 2025, Canada imposed retaliatory measures, causing Canadian imports of U.S. alcoholic beverages to plummet by approximately $581 million, or 81 percent, in a one year period compared to a similar period the year prior. “Instead of focusing our energy on outcompeting rivals like China, the Trump administration has unwisely chosen to pick a damaging and cost-spiking tariff fight with our closest ally and biggest trading partner, Canada. And that is deeply damaging to this industry and to the Upstate economy in general, which borders Canada,” said Senator Schumer . At the same time, changing national consumption patterns are creating new challenges for New York’s wine industry, requiring local growers and producers to adapt to a changing marketplace and face increased competition. Schumer said higher costs, downturns in consumption, and the loss of access to much of the Canadian market have major regional consequences on the craft beverage industry. These challenges have been further compounded by four logistics disruptions in the past six months. In March 2026, the closure of DNT Express, a Clyde-based freight forwarder that served Finger Lakes wineries, eliminated a critical logistics provider. In May, Manhattan Beer & Beverage acquired the Opici Wine Distributor’s New York portfolio, affecting Finger Lakes wineries and creating another major distribution transition. In July, national beverage distributor RNDC filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy, adding further uncertainty to an already strained distribution system. Lastly, the closure of the historic Pleasant Valley Wine Company eliminated another important regional storage and distribution resource. Together, these disruptions have left producers scrambling for reliable freight forwarding, cold storage, and distribution capacity. To help address these challenges, Schumer announced his support for the New York Wine & Grape Foundation’s application for $500,000 through the U.S. Small Business Administration’s Supply Chain Acceleration and Logistics Enablement (SCALE) Program to support the marketing research, business modeling, governance, financial analysis, and legal planning needed to evaluate a multi-beverage logistics cooperative serving New York’s wine, beer, spirits and cider producers. A cooperative could help restore reliable storage and shipping capacity, expand market access, and strengthen supply chain resilience. Schumer said the Schuyler County Business Park underscores the importance of strategic federal investment in Upstate communities, with the park serving as a platform for economic development in the Southern Tier, including the growth of the region’s craft beverage industry, such as Lucky Hare Brewing Company. Schumer previously visited the business park in 2023 to promote the bipartisan ONSHORE Act, which sought to strengthen industrial sites, infrastructure, and workforce development so rural communities can attract businesses and critical supply chains. Schumer’s letter to the Administrator of the U.S. Small Business Administration, Kelly Loeffler, can be found HERE or below: Dear Administrator Loeffler, I am pleased to write in strong support of the New York Wine & Grape Foundation’s application for $500,000 through the U.S. Small Business Administration’s Supply Chain Acceleration and Logistics Enablement (SCALE) Program. This funding will enable the Foundation to conduct a comprehensive feasibility study for a producer-owned logistics cooperative serving New York’s wine, beer, spirits, and cider producers. Established by New York State in 1985 as an economic development entity, the New York Wine & Grape Foundation has the statewide industry, relationships, authority, and technical capacity necessary to coordinate this effort. New York’s craft beverage producers – particularly small and mid-sized businesses in the Finger Lakes and other rural communities across Upstate New York – have been hit by overlapping losses in freight-forwarding, cold-storage, and distribution capacity. The foundation has brought craft beverage associations together around a collaborative response and is well-positioned to develop a durable solution that strengthens market access and supply-chain resilience. If awarded, the foundation will complete the marketing research, business modeling, governance design, financial analysis, and legal planning needed to evaluate and establish a multi-beverage logistics cooperative. A successful cooperative would restore reliable storage and shipping capacity, expand access to markets, and help New York producers across the industry remain competitive. For additional information, please do not hesitate to contact me or my Grants Director, Kaia Moore, in my Washington office at grants@schumer.senate.gov . Thank you for your consideration. ###

Schumer Secured Federal Investment To Expand Access To Affordable Healthcare In Yates County, Nursing Care, Occupational Therapy, Social Work Counseling, Athletic Training, Physical Therapy, And Wellness Coaching To Rural Communities New Clinic Will Serve ~1,000 Rural Residents And Create Hands-On Health Care Training Opportunities For 100 College Students Each Year Schumer: New Clinic Is Win-Win For Yates County Families And Keuka College Students After launching his push to deliver federal funding three years ago, U.S. Senator Chuck Schumer today joined Keuka College leaders to cut the ribbon on the College’s new Rural Community Outpatient Clinic. The planned clinic will address a critical need in a county with limited health care resources by providing area residents with healthcare services including nursing care, occupational therapy, social work counseling, athletic training, physical therapy, and wellness coaching. The new clinic will also strengthen career pathways and help prepare the next generation of health care professionals to serve the region by giving Keuka College students hands-on clinical training opportunities. Schumer celebrated the opening of this community facility and pledged to keep fighting for more federal resources to strengthen rural health care access across the Finger Lakes region. “When Keuka College leaders came to me asking for help to build a new Rural Community Outpatient Clinic, I promised I wouldn’t stop fighting until they got every penny they needed to build the health care facility the community deserves. I’m proud to be here today after delivering $1.6 million in federal funding for this critical project and to say a promise made is a promise kept,” said Senator Schumer. “Today, we don’t just cut a ribbon. We open a door for 1,000 rural residents in the surrounding community who can now access needed health care services and the hundreds of Keuka College students who can get the clinical training opportunities they need to become healthcare professionals. I will always fight to ensure New York’s rural communities have the resources they need to access affordable health care services.” Keuka College President Amy Storey said, “ Keuka College is grateful to Senator Schumer for his leadership and for securing the federal funding that helped make this vision a reality. This clinic represents an important investment in the health and well-being of rural communities while creating valuable opportunities for Keuka College students – the next generation of healthcare professionals – to learn and serve. We are proud to partner with Senator Schumer and others throughout our region to expand access to clinical services and prepare students to meet the healthcare needs of the future.” The senator fought to deliver the necessary funding for Keuka College to create its Rural Community Outpatient Clinic. In September 2023, Schumer stood in Yates County to successfully push for $1.6 million in federal funding through the FY2024 Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies budget bill to move the project over the finish line and get rural Yates County residents the healthcare facility they deserve. The clinic will be a one-stop shop for health care and wellness services. Schumer explained the clinic will be a win-win for the community, training much-needed new nurses and healthcare workers while serving an additional ~1,000 area residents. The establishment of this comprehensive clinic will also support enrollment at Keuka College by providing clinical training opportunities for 100 students per year in the College’s healthcare programs. According to Keuka College, approximately 85% of alumni remain in New York after graduation, making a significant contribution to the state's healthcare workforce. Schumer underscored that strengthening career pathways and helping prepare the next generation of healthcare professionals to serve the region is vital. In 2025, a report that examined shortages in health professionals in 16 rural counties–including Yates–identified low rates of health care providers as well as a lack of access to basic care in many counties. Schumer emphasized that the creation of the rural outpatient clinic will provide access to a variety of affordable healthcare in an area that lacks sufficient services within a 30-mile radius. ###

After Previously Helping Deliver $3.9 Million To Establish The Cemetery In 2023, Schumer’s Push Now Includes $3 Million For Critical Gateway, Entrance, Safety & Accessibility Upgrades At New York State Veterans Cemetery – Finger Lakes In Upcoming Budget Bill Schumer Also Announces Push for $2 Million Pending VA Grants To Add 300 New Burial Plots, Fencing & Lighting, Stormwater Infrastructure, And To Maintain & Care For Veteran Headstones Schumer: Honor Our Heroes With The Resting Place They Deserve Standing with local Veterans at the New York State Veterans Cemetery – Finger Lakes in Romulus, New York, U.S. Senator Chuck Schumer today launched his push to secure nearly $5 million in federal funding to expand, modernize, and improve New York’s first state veterans cemetery. Schumer explained the funding would upgrade the cemetery’s gateway and entrance, expand cemetery capacity, and preserve the dignity of the cemetery’s sacred grounds. “New York State Veterans Cemetery in the Finger Lakes, located at the former Sampson military base, is hallowed ground, rooted in the history of hundreds of thousands of World War II and Korean War-era service members who trained here before going on to defend our nation. As we celebrate our country’s 250 th anniversary this year, we must honor the service and sacrifices of Americans who have served in the armed forces,” said Senator Schumer. “That is why I am here today to launch my push for nearly $5 million in federal support to make critical upgrades to this historic veterans cemetery. I was proud to help deliver the pivotal funding needed to establish this cemetery as New York’s first-ever state veterans cemetery, but that was only the first step. Now, the cemetery is in need of greater burial capacity and resources to care for the headstones of these heroes, as well as safety, accessibility, and infrastructure upgrades. I’m proud to launch my push for over $5 million to ensure that our nation’s veterans have the dignified resting place they have earned after fighting to protect our freedom.” Located in Seneca County, New York – the birthplace of Memorial Day – New York State Veterans Cemetery – Finger Lakes is a nationally-recognized memorial that honors hundreds of thousands of veterans, including 33 Purple Heart recipients connected to the historic Sampson military installations, who trained and served our nation. Originally built in 1942 as a U.S. Naval Training Station, the site housed the Sampson College for returning GI Bill veterans from 1946 to 1949, and then later served as the Sampson Air Force Basic Military Training Center before being largely decommissioned in 1956. The site is now home to the New York State Veterans Cemetery – Finger Lakes, and is the resting place for Armed Forces veterans, their spouses, and their children. There are additionally 33 interred Purple Heart recipients and veterans connected to the historic Sampson Military Installations. Chairman of the Friends of the New York State Veterans Cemetery—Finger Lakes, Michael F. Nozzolio, NY State Senator, ret. said, “ The Friends of the New York State Veterans Cemetery—Finger Lakes are extremely grateful and pleased our United States Senator Chuck Schumer will support and advocate for funds to enhance the permanent resting place that honors all our Nation’s veterans. Senator Schumer’s advocacy in the United States Senate is critically important for the approval of the New York State Department of Veterans’ Services grant request that will make the first New York State Veterans Cemetery safer, more secure, and create easier access for senior citizens and the disabled, providing many more the opportunity to honor the veterans of our United States Armed Forces.” The current entrance is functionally obsolete and no longer provides safe, secure, or accessible access for visitors. Schumer today announced his push for $3 million in federal funding in the Fiscal Year 2027 Transportation, Housing and Urban Development appropriations bill to create a safer and more accessible gateway. The new proposed entrance will have improved lighting and signage to boost public safety and protect a significant asset for New York State through secure, well-defined infrastructure. Schumer explained that most of the cemetery’s visitors, including surviving spouses and siblings, are predominantly older adults who often have mobility limitations. The senator explained that the proposed upgrades are necessary to safely serve this population and give our veterans the resting place they deserve. In addition to the $3 million, Schumer also today announced he is pushing the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) National Cemetery Administration to approve New York State’s applications for two Veterans Cemetery grants, which together would provide over $2 million in additional federal support for cemetery expansion, infrastructure improvements, and headstone maintenance. The Cemetery is now eligible to apply for and receive these VA grants thanks to efforts by Schumer and state and local leaders in 2023, when Schumer helped deliver $3.9 million in federal funding needed to finally establish the New York State Veterans Cemetery – Finger Lakes as New York State’s first-ever veterans cemetery. The cemetery is thus eligible to pursue future federal VA grants as one of the 120 VA-designated state and tribal veteran cemeteries that may be financially supported through the Federal VA Veterans Cemetery Grants Program. The proposed grants will support the construction of 300 additional burial crypts, expanding the Cemetery’s long-term capacity and allowing more veterans and eligible family members to be laid to rest in a place dedicated to honoring their service. This expanded capacity will also provide more Gold Star Families and loved ones with a permanent place to gather, reflect, and pay tribute. Additionally, the project will upgrade stormwater infrastructure, construct new fencing and update signage to improve navigation, and enhance the experience of families visiting to honor loved ones. Funding will also be used to preserve the cemetery’s appearance and integrity by raising, realigning, cleaning, and rehabilitating headstones. Maintaining these sacred grounds is essential to ensuring every veteran is remembered in a setting that reflects the dignity of their service. Together, these grants will expand the Cemetery’s capacity while ensuring it remains a lasting tribute to those who served our nation. In addition to the NYS Veteran Cemetery at the former Sampson military base, Schumer also secured a total of $46 million from 2016-2019 to construct and establish the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) National Western New York Veterans Cemetery in Genesee County, New York in 2020, bringing a much-needed veterans cemetery to Western New York to serve the 80,000 WNY veterans who then lacked a veterans cemetery within 100 miles of their home. ###

Lake Erie Region Is Largest Grape Growing Area East Of Rocky Mountains – Supporting 2,000 Jobs – But Earlier This Year Major NY Grape Processor Abruptly Canceled Contracts With Western NY Farmers Schumer Explains USDA Has Authority To Purchase Excess Grapes For Domestic Food Assistance Programs & Help Keep Upstate Concord Grape Farmers Growing Schumer To USDA: Buy Juice And Boost Growers! As Western New York grape farmers are facing growing uncertainty – after their contracts for this season were suddenly terminated – U.S. Senator Chuck Schumer stood at the Cornell Lake Erie Research and Extension Laboratory and called on the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) to purchase concord grape juice for use by domestic nutrition programs across the country. Earlier this year, Refresco suddenly canceled contracts with approximately 126 farmers across New York and Pennsylvania after they had already invested in preparing their vineyards for this season, leaving local growers in a lurch. Schumer is pushing the USDA to help Western New York’s farmers, many of whom rely on contracts with Refresco, by purchasing some of this surplus product to ensure the continued success of Concord grape growers in New York. “Upstate New York is known for the top-notch quality of our Concord grapes, which are made into everything from juices to jellies and are an important part of our state’s agricultural economy. But earlier this year, on top of skyrocketing costs, many Western New York farmers had their Concord grape contracts cancelled by Refresco, leaving growers in a lurch and without the certainty they rely on to know they’ll have a market for their harvest,” said Senator Schumer. “That’s why I’m calling on the USDA to buy Concord grape juice for domestic nutrition programs and boost our growers because when the farmers who feed our families need help from forces beyond their control, we need to act. I’ve worked with USDA on surplus grape purchases before, and I’m urging the USDA to again provide certainty to Upstate farmers, put American-grown grapes to good use, and strengthen the domestic food supply chain we all depend on. It’s a win-win-win.” Chautauqua County is the leading grape-producing county in the state and the largest grape-growing county in the country outside of California. Every year, about 800 growers produce 150,000 tons or more of grapes on more than 22,000 acres on the Lake Erie Plain across northern Pennsylvania and Western New York. Products like juices and jellies that come from Concord grapes are processed locally and sold across the world. The Cornell Cooperative Extension estimates that the Lake Erie Grape Belt region supports about 2,000 jobs, contributes upwards of $300 million in economic impact, and supports a fruit and vegetable processing industry that employs over 5,000 workers. “Our grape growers are an important part of Chautauqua County’s agricultural heritage and local economy, and we appreciate our federal partners, including Senator Schumer, for recognizing the challenges facing our growers and working to support them ,” said Chautauqua County Executive PJ Wendel. “The grape industry supports thousands of jobs and contributes significantly to our regional economy, making it important that we continue to work together to ensure our growers have the resources and support they need to remain successful. We are grateful for the continued advocacy and partnership of our federal representatives as we work to strengthen and protect the future of the grape industry throughout the Lake Erie Grape Belt.” "We are grateful to Senator Schumer for stepping up for our growers during this unprecedented crisis,” said New York Wine and Grape Foundation Executive Director Sam Filler. “The immediate relief a Section 32 purchase would provide is essential—but we also recognize that the Concord grape industry needs a long-term strategic roadmap to build resilience. That's why we're excited about the potential for Specialty Crop Block Grant funding that we expect to be announced this Fall to support comprehensive industry planning. Together, these investments—emergency relief now, plus strategic planning for tomorrow—give us the real opportunity to turn this crisis into a catalyst for innovation and sustainable growth in the Lake Erie Grape Belt." “New York Farm Bureau appreciates Senator Chuck Schumer’s support of New York grape growers in the Lake Erie region, who suffered the abrupt loss of market earlier this year due to Refresco’s cancellation of contracts. This loss of market has already posed a substantial economic risk to growers. If USDA were to purchase these grapes through Section 32 funds, it would not only provide immediate relief to New York grape growers, but it would also allow grapes to be included in the school lunch program. With harvest season quickly approaching, the time is now to help our New York grape growers,” said David Fisher, President of the New York Farm Bureau. “For 150 years, the western New York grape industry has grown in good economic times and endured through challenging times because of the strong partnership between the western New York family farmers, university research and extension personnel, and local, state, and federal legislatures. Currently, global grape over-production is depressing our local market and this is when the industry-university-government relationship is needed most. We are appreciative of the support from Senator Schumer for programs to purchase surplus juice for domestic programs and to support innovative research through the Specialty Crop Research Initiative are critical for the industry to thrive and grow into the future,” said Dr. Terry Bates, Director of Cornell Lake Erie Research and Extension Lab and Cornell AgriTech “Our growers have faced real headwinds these past few seasons, and this kind of federal support makes a tangible difference. Across Chautauqua County and the local region, 126 farms across 2,500 acres of Concord grapes were affected by the sudden loss of a processor contract, putting these farms and businesses at serious risk. We’re grateful to Senator Schumer for recognizing the importance of the Concord grape industry to Chautauqua County and for pushing the USDA to act,” said Robert Patterson, Jr., President, Chautauqua County Farm Bureau and Westfield Maid Cooperative. “As the owner of multiple agr-businesses, I am experiencing the economic ripple-effects of canceled grape contracts by multiple processors. My vineyard operation will have in excess of 600 tons of grapes with no home this fall, and my equipment dealership is suffering as a result of numerous customers facing steep financial losses due to canceled grape contracts. Rising input costs in 2026 due to a trade war and an apparently endless Iranian war have made for very difficult times in the Agricultural sector. Senator Schumer’s efforts working in conjunction with the USDA to assist with the current oversupply issue is greatly appreciated and prove that some lawmakers still care about our nation's food supply and the well-being of those who produce those products,” said Chad Schofield, owner of Schofield Farms LLC, Westfield Ag and Turf, Affinity Agriculture LLC, and Repurposed Organics, LLC. Western New York’s grape industry is an economic anchor for the state’s agricultural industry, as Lake Erie’s shallow depth extends the growing season by moderating temperatures as it keeps air moving when grapes are at risk for frost. The region extends far beyond Chautauqua County. Niagara County is home to the Niagara Escarpment American Viticultural Area, which contains nearly 60 farms across more than 1,000 acres of vineyard. The Niagara grape was created in Niagara County by cross-breeding Concord and Cassady grapes and is now a staple for making white grape juice. In March, Refresco, a major processor for many New York grape farmers, canceled all of its contracts with grape growers. Refresco bought from 126 grape growers across New York and Pennsylvania in the Lake Erie region. Since then, New York’s grape growers have been struggling in the face of an uncertain future. Schumer explained in a letter to USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins that purchasing grapes for use by domestic nutrition programs will alleviate stress for Concord grape growers in Western New York who now do not have a buyer for their crops. Section 32 funds are authorized by Section 32 of the Agricultural Adjustment Act of 1933 and used by USDA to purchase agricultural products, which are in turn used for nutrition programs such as the school lunch program. These “bonus buys” have been used by USDA in the past to stabilize agricultural markets, support communities, and deliver nutritious food to those who need it most. In fact, earlier this year, Schumer fought to secure exactly such a purchase by USDA to stabilize prices for New York grape farmers. Section 32 has also been deployed successfully for Concord grapes in 2006, 2007, 2009, 2014, 2017, and 2024. Schumer explained farmers are also facing rising costs across the board. A recent report from New York State showed the state’s farmers faced increased expenses of $20,000 annually. According to a recent report from the U.S. Congress Joint Economic Committee – Minority, the average farmer spent as much as $1,500 more to refill their farm’s on-site fuel tank compared to the same high point during the 2025 planting season. In New York, it cost $1,494 more to fill up a typical farm fuel tank, $199 more to fill up a typical grain truck, and $243 more to fill up a typical tractor compared to last year. The New York Farm Bureau revealed fertilizer prices have skyrocketed since last year, from approximately $400 a ton to $580 a ton, a more than 40% increase, with anhydrous ammonia now over $1,000 a ton. Farmers across the country have reported delaying or even forgoing fertilizer purchases due to cost spikes, leading them to plant fewer acres and risk future profits. ###

Schumer Says Effort Will Strengthen Regional Healthcare Ecosystem, Meet Growing Demand For Healthcare Workers, And Support Good-Paying Jobs Across Allegany, Steuben & Livingston Counties Alfred State Partners With Jones Memorial, St. James, And Noyes Memorial Hospitals To Provide Hands-On Training And Help More Students Advance In Healthcare Careers Schumer: Federal Funding Will Help Strengthen Rural Healthcare And Expand Access To Skilled Professionals Across Upstate NY U.S. Senator Chuck Schumer today visited Alfred State College to launch a push in support of the college's new proposal to strengthen the regional healthcare workforce. Schumer called on the U.S. Department of Labor to deliver $6,197,191 in federal funding to expand healthcare education and training, strengthen career pathways to good-paying jobs, and prepare the next generation of healthcare professionals to address critical staffing shortages in rural communities across Upstate New York, including Allegany, Steuben, and Livingston counties. “From the classroom to the clinic, this innovative healthcare program will strengthen the regional healthcare system and help address critical staffing shortages,” said Senator Schumer. “At a time when rural healthcare systems across Upstate New York are facing significant pressures, from cuts to critical programs and federal policies creating even greater uncertainty, it is vital that we invest in preparing a pipeline of the next generation of healthcare workers. I’m proud to support Alfred State College’s proposal, in partnership with hospitals and healthcare facilities from across the region, to prepare over 500 people for healthcare careers in Western New York.” Last month, Schumer explained in a letter to Acting U.S. Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling that the college’s proposal, titled “Curriculum to Career: Expanding the Healthcare Workforce in Rural Western New York ,” would directly address workforce shortages in nursing, radiology, healthcare management, and more. The effort will create new pathways to healthcare education and good-paying jobs while also addressing the shortage of healthcare professionals. By expanding clinical placements, paid internships, on-the-job training, healthcare program enrollment, and stackable credentials, the project will help more students move from the classroom into the healthcare workforce. Alfred State College projects the initiative will help 543 participants start an accredited training and/or degree-seeking education. The effort comes as rural healthcare systems and communities across Upstate New York face significant pressures, from cuts to critical programs to policies creating greater uncertainty. A 2025 report examining healthcare professional shortages in 16 rural New York counties identified major healthcare gaps—including practitioners, providers, and physical facilities—in rural counties such as Allegany, Steuben, Cattaraugus, and Wyoming. "We are deeply grateful to Senator Schumer for his steadfast leadership and unwavering advocacy for Alfred State College and rural Western New York. Welcoming him alongside our vital regional partners at Jones Memorial, St. James, and Noyes Hospitals underscores our shared commitment to solving the healthcare workforce shortage in Allegany, Steuben, and Livingston counties. With the $6.2 million support from the WORC Grant, our Curriculum to Career initiative will allow us to expand clinical placements, launch hands-on training and microcredentials, and prepare the next generation of essential healthcare professionals right here in our community,” said Dr. Steven A. Mauro, President of Alfred State College. “Developing a workforce pipeline and providing career development through education are key business and recruitment/retention focus areas for Noyes Health. This grant, and the partnership with Alfred State will significantly enhance our ability to attract, retain, and grow talent in our region to develop the healthcare workforce of the next generation. We greatly appreciate the leadership at Alfred State and Senator Schumer’s support in this coming to fruition,” said J. Chad Teeters, MD, MBA, MS, FACC, President/CEO, UR Medicine - Noyes Health. “St. James Hospital is incredibly thankful for Senator Schumer's dedication to addressing the unique challenges faced by rural healthcare providers. His leadership in advocating for workforce training grants will have a profound and lasting impact, allowing us to expand access to quality care, improve health outcomes, and create sustainable career pathways for individuals in our rural areas. Support of workforce investment grants is a testament to his commitment to the well-being of all constituents and our community,” said Wendy Disbrow, MBA, RN, President and CEO of St. James Hospital. “The years following the pandemic taught us that we cannot solve gaps in the rural workforce by working in silos. It takes a joint effort by employers and educators along with resource support. The Workforce Opportunity for Rural Communities (WORC) initiative is vital for institutions like ours. It will allow us to fill the skilled healthcare labor gaps, leveraging the local rural workforce and in turn strengthening economic development,” said James Helms, FACHE, FHFMA, CPA, President / CEO of Jones Memorial Hospital. Schumer explained that the proposal will help build a stronger healthcare pipeline by giving students and current healthcare workers more opportunities to gain the skills and experience needed by local employers. Alfred State College will work with three regionally significant healthcare partners: Jones Memorial Hospital in Wellsville, St. James Hospital in Hornell, and Noyes Memorial Hospital in Dansville. The initiative will provide on-the-job training for healthcare workers, expand the number of clinical placements, and provide paid summer internships for students enrolled in healthcare majors. These hands-on opportunities will help students and workers gain valuable experience while giving local healthcare providers a stronger and sustained pipeline of skilled talent. It will also increase enrollment in healthcare programs at Alfred State College among both traditional students and adult learners. In 2025, the incoming class at Alfred State College reached 1,493 full-time new students on census date, the largest group since 2010, for a total enrollment of 3,758, with most degree-seeking undergraduate students being in-state students from across New York. Schumer previously delivered federal investment to support successful industry-based workforce training programs at Alfred State. In 2021, Schumer announced $1.4 million in federal funding to meet training needs like specialized welding skills for two major industrial employers in the region and support nearly 200 new jobs. Schumer explained that two of the counties—Allegany and Steuben—in the project area are part of the federally designated Appalachian region and have faced high levels of poverty, low job growth, and health disparities. Workforce Opportunity and Innovation Act (WORC) grants, through the U.S. Department of Labor, in partnership with the Appalachian Regional Commission, allow recipients to help their communities diversify their local economies by developing a skilled workforce and providing equitable access to marginalized communities. Schumer’s letter to Acting Secretary of Labor Keith Sonderling can be found HERE or below: Dear Acting Secretary Sonderling, I am pleased to write in support of the application submitted by Alfred State College of Technology to the U.S. Department of Labor’s Workforce Opportunity for Rural Communities (WORC) Initiative. SUNY Alfred’s proposal, “Curriculum to Career: Expanding the Healthcare Workforce in Rural Western New York,” will directly addresses workforce shortages in nursing, radiology, and healthcare management that impair the quality of healthcare received by rural residents. As Western New York’s leading technical college, Alfred State is uniquely positioned to continue helping grow the region’s workforce. This collaborative effort between Alfred State College, local hospitals, and workforce development agencies will result in an increased and improved pipeline of healthcare workers across New York’s Appalachian Region. Alfred State will provide summer internships for students enrolled in healthcare majors, provide an increased number of clinical placements, and implement stackable degree pathways through micro-credential and certificate programs. The proposal will also serve current healthcare workers by providing on-the-job training, flexible course delivery, and tuition support to allow providers the opportunity to develop additional skills while working. Quality healthcare is the bedrock for a healthy community, especially in rural areas. The Southern Tier, at the northern tip of Appalachia, continues to be one of the most economically distressed areas of the Northeast. This project offers an opportunity to reverse this trend by building on SUNY Alfred’s existing technical curriculum. I applaud Alfred State College of Technology for its foresight, and sincerely hope their application is met with your approval. If you have questions, please do not hesitate to contact me or my Grants Director at grants@schumer.senate.gov . Thank you for your consideration. ###
